summary: Orbit Arch: Near-Earth Asteroid Planner is a browser game where you play a NASA mission designer launching a CubeSat to intercept a real near-Earth asteroid. Choose from five targets, including Bennu, Apophis and Ryugu, and split limited points between fuel, solar panels and shielding. Plot your launch window and use Earth gravity assists to save Δv while avoiding radiation belts and solar flares. A live orbital simulation, medals and scoring keep it replayable. Orbital parameters are derived from NASA JPL Horizons, and all graphics and audio are procedurally generated in a single HTML file.
details:
What it does and how it works

Orbit Architect is a browser game that puts players in the role of a NASA mission designer. They pick a real near-Earth asteroid (Apophis, Ryugu, Bennu, Eros or Didymos), split 100 points between fuel (Δv), solar panels and radiation shielding, then choose a launch day, launch Δv and burn angle. A live N-body-style simulation (Sun and Earth gravity, integrated with velocity-Verlet) previews the trajectory and the predicted closest approach before launch. In flight, players make small course corrections, use Earth gravity assists to gain free Δv, and manage battery, radiation dose and fuel. They fail if they run out of fuel or power, absorb too much radiation, hit the Sun, or miss the mission window. A “Suggest Window” tool searches launch dates and angles to help beginners.

Benefits and intended impact

The game makes mission-design trade-offs tangible: launch windows, delta-v budgets, gravity assists, solar power falling off with distance, and radiation hazards. Players learn why real missions like OSIRIS-REx, Hayabusa2 and DART needed careful planning, and why near-Earth asteroids matter for science and planetary defense. It needs no install or account, so it works in classrooms and on phones.

Tools and technology

It is a single self-contained HTML file built with vanilla JavaScript, HTML5 Canvas 2D and CSS. Sound effects are synthesized live with the Web Audio API, and best scores are saved in localStorage. No external libraries, images or audio files are used. Orbital parameters (semi-major axis, eccentricity, longitude of perihelion) are rounded values derived from NASA JPL Horizons / SBDB, with attribution shown in the game footer and Data Source screen.
